opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, partly because I think it's one of the most underrated skills in research, and one of the things I see junior researchers struggle with most.

The core thing I'd say is that research is a very heavy-tailed activity. Most of the ideas you could work on will go nowhere, and a small number will turn out to be really valuable. So the question isn't just "is this a good idea?" It's "is this the best use of my next few weeks, given everything else I could be doing?" A lot of people have a reasonable-sounding idea, start on it, and then just keep going because they've started, without asking whether it's still the most promising thing.

One framing I like is to think in terms of information gain per unit time. Early in a project, you should be optimising for learning as fast as possible whether your idea is any good. That means running the quick-and-dirty experiment before the beautiful rigorous one, looking at the data yourself, and trying to get a signal in days rather than months. In machine learning especially, you can often get a surprisingly clear answer from a small model or a cheap proxy. If it looks promising, then you invest in rigour.

I also think it's worth separating a few modes of research. There's an exploration phase, where you're trying to build intuition and you don't really know what the question is yet. There's an understanding phase, where you have hypotheses and you're testing them. And there's a distillation phase, where you're trying to turn what you've learned into something that convinces other people. These need quite different mindsets, and a common failure is getting stuck in one: endlessly exploring without committing, or prematurely trying to write a polished paper before you actually understand what's going on.

Then there's the bigger-picture question of which directions to pick at all. For me, coming from the angle of interpretability and AI safety, I try to ask: if this works really well, what does it actually change? Does it help us understand or make safer the kinds of systems we're actually worried about? It's very easy to work on something that's intellectually fun, and I'm very susceptible to that, but that doesn't map onto real-world impact. I've tried to become more pragmatic over time, asking what problems people genuinely need solved, rather than what's most elegant.

And finally, I'd say be willing to kill projects. Sunk cost is brutal in research. Setting explicit checkpoints, like "in two weeks, if I haven't seen X, I'll seriously reconsider," helps a lot. Having a mentor or collaborator you check in with regularly is also enormously valuable, because it's much easier to see someone else's project is stuck than your own.

r002.rationale: It mentions junior researchers' struggles and sunk-cost pressure, but does not frame acting under uncertainty itself as a psychological challenge.

r003.rationale: The response distinguishes exploration, understanding, and distillation, and discusses choosing directions, but does not identify deciding whether to investigate a problem more deeply or step back for a broader view as part of prioritisation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think prioritisation is one of the most important and most neglected skills in research, and honestly it's something I was pretty bad at for a long time. The core thing I'd say is that in research, the variance in how much different projects matter is enormous. It's not like some projects are 20% better than others — it's more like the best projects are ten or a hundred times more valuable than the median project. And that means that the question of "what should I work on?" is often more important than the question of "how well am I executing on it?"

The way I actually think about it in practice is roughly in two stages. The first is exploration: you want to spend a meaningful chunk of your time just looking at lots of possible directions cheaply. Read widely, poke at things for a day or two, run quick and dirty experiments, talk to people. The goal here isn't to produce anything, it's to get information about which directions are promising. I think a lot of people, especially early on, skip this step because it feels unproductive — you don't have anything to show for it. But you're buying information about which bets are worth making, and that's incredibly valuable.

The second stage is exploitation: once you've found something that seems promising, you commit and go deep. And here the key skill is noticing when your initial excitement was wrong. It's very easy to get sunk-cost-ed into a project because you've spent three weeks on it, when actually the right move is to drop it. I try to have fairly explicit checkpoints — like, "if I haven't seen signal X by the end of the week, I'll seriously reconsider."

Something I'd emphasise for people doing mechanistic interpretability specifically, or really any field that's young and fast-moving, is that the space of valuable problems is way bigger than the number of people working on them. So you don't need to find the single best problem; you need to avoid the trap of working on something that's either already crowded or just doesn't matter. A useful heuristic I use is: "if this project goes perfectly, who cares and why?" If I can't give a clear answer, that's a red flag. And the other side: "what's the fastest, cheapest experiment that would tell me this whole direction is doomed?" Doing that experiment first saves you a lot of pain.

The other thing I'd say — and this is a bit more meta — is that your own taste gets better with practice, and you should treat it as a skill to develop rather than something fixed. Early on, borrow heavily from people whose judgment you trust: a mentor, a supervisor, people in the field whose work you admire. Ask them not just what's interesting but why they think it's interesting, and try to build a model of their reasoning. Over time you'll start disagreeing with them in places, and that's when you know you've actually developed your own taste.

And finally, I'd push back gently on the idea that you need to get this perfectly right. The cost of working on a slightly suboptimal thing for a few months isn't that high if you're learning and getting feedback. The real failure mode is either freezing because you can't decide, or spending a year on something you had a nagging feeling was wrong from month two. So: explore cheaply, commit when you've got signal, have explicit kill criteria, and keep asking yourself whether anyone would care if it worked.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about which research projects are valuable, but does not say that research requires greater ability to act under uncertainty than other kinds of work.

r002.rationale: It presents research prioritisation as psychologically difficult: the speaker says they were bad at it, describes sunk-cost attachment and misplaced excitement, and identifies freezing or ignoring doubts as failure modes.

r003.rationale: The response explicitly contrasts broadly exploring directions cheaply with committing to a promising direction and going deep, presenting these as stages of prioritisation.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: what would actually change if this research succeeded? It’s quite easy to find a problem that’s technically interesting, that you know how to make progress on, and then spend six months on it without ever really asking why the answer matters.

I’d try to work backwards from the thing you care about. If that’s making AI safer, what’s a concrete way your research could help? Who would use the result, and what would they do differently? You don’t need a completely convincing story upfront — research is uncertain — but you should have some story you can interrogate.

Then there’s tractability and your personal fit. A question can be incredibly important, but if you have no way of getting evidence about it, that’s a problem. I like looking for small experiments that could tell you whether an approach has promise, before committing to a huge project.

And I think prioritisation should be an ongoing process. As you learn things, you should be willing to say, ‘Actually, the motivation for this project no longer makes sense.’ That’s emotionally difficult when you’ve invested a lot in it, but discovering that you should work on something else can itself be valuable progress.

r001.rationale: The response says research is uncertain, but does not state that research requires more ability to act under uncertainty than other kinds of work.

r002.rationale: It notes that research is uncertain and that changing direction after investing in a project is emotionally difficult, framing uncertainty-driven prioritisation as a psychological challenge.

r003.rationale: It discusses working backwards from goals and using small experiments, but does not identify choosing between investigating a problem more deeply and stepping back for a broader view.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to be explicit about what you’re trying to achieve. It’s very easy in machine learning to gravitate towards a problem because there’s a benchmark, you know how to get started, and you can imagine a paper at the end. But that doesn’t necessarily mean that solving it would be useful.

For me, the motivating goal is making advanced AI safer. So I want to ask: if this research succeeds, what would we understand or be able to do that we can’t do now? And why would that help? In mechanistic interpretability, for example, producing an interesting explanation of a model’s behaviour can be valuable, but there’s a further question of whether the methods could help us identify or fix something consequential.

Then I’d weigh that against tractability and how much I can contribute. A very important problem isn’t automatically a good project if I have no way to make progress on it. I like finding a small, concrete experiment that tests an assumption behind a bigger research direction. That gives you information fairly quickly, including information that might tell you to stop.

And I think that last bit matters a lot: prioritisation isn’t just choosing a project at the start. It’s being willing to update when the work stops looking promising, rather than continuing because you’ve already invested three months in it.
